claims.text: A carefully optimized post-synthesis annealing treatment can promote controlled solute segregation to grain boundaries.
Controlled grain-boundary segregation produced by annealing will improve high-temperature creep resistance.
Controlled grain-boundary segregation produced by annealing will improve high-temperature tensile strength.
The annealing treatment will not increase alloy density.
The annealing treatment will not degrade room-temperature performance.
The starting material is a standard single-phase polycrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy based on refractory elements such as Mo, Nb, Ta, and W.
The tailored annealing or thermomechanical schedule can induce minor grain-boundary segregation while avoiding significant secondary-phase precipitation.
The proposed benefit should hold under tensile or creep loading at approximately 900–1200 °C.
The treatment modifies grain-boundary composition and structure through controlled solute segregation.
Localized enrichment of selected solutes at grain boundaries increases intergranular cohesion.
Increased intergranular cohesion suppresses grain-boundary sliding and diffusion-controlled high-temperature deformation.
Because annealing does not alter bulk composition, density remains unchanged.
Because annealing does not alter bulk composition, room-temperature mechanical properties remain unchanged.
The treated alloy will have appreciably higher elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will show no significant change in room-temperature ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated baseline has limited high-temperature strength and creep resistance but acceptable room-temperature properties.
Excessive annealing or aggressive thermomechanical processing can cause precipitation or grain coarsening that degrades high- and room-temperature performance.
